newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee called to open flat to 1.00 cent lower.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee called to open flat to 1.00 cent lower.

text.p: CSCE coffee futures were called to open unchanged to 1.00 cent per lb lower on Thursday, as the market is expected to take a breather after Wednesday's steep run-up, traders said.
New York arabica futures surged on Wednesday, as news the ACPC planned to keep export quotas intact sparked a flurry of speculative buying.

July arabicas shot up 12.85 cents per lb -- more than five percent -- on the day, to end at 253.10 cents, after ranging from 255.00 and 239.00 cents. Second-position September jumped 10.35 cents to 225.05 cents, while the outer months finished up 3.80 to 6.60.

On Wednesday, the 14-nation ACPC reached an accord to limits export quotas at 52.75 million bags for one year starting July 1. This compared with a cap for 1996/97 orginally set at 53.55 million 60-kg bags but later reduced by 800,000 bags.

Traders are continuing their weather watch in top-grower Brazil. A strong cold front will come northward out of Argentina during the next few days, bringing the coolest weather of the early season to Brazil's coffee belt, but no damaging cold is expected, private forecaster Weather Services Corp said Thursday.
Technically, traders pegged initial July resistance at Wednesday's high of 255.00 cents, with a key upside target at 262.00 cents. Near-term July support was seen at 250.00 cents.

After Wednesday's close, the CSCE reported certified coffee stocks continued to climb. Stocks increased by 2,250 bags, to 51,212 bags as of May 20. There was no coffee pending grading, the exchange said.
London July robusta futures were up at midday Thursday, but off highs. LIFFE July rose $40 at the break, to $2,130, after reaching a peak of $2,145.

Elsewhere, French coffee consumption is expected to fall in 1997, mostly the result of higher retail prices, the chairman of the French coffee industry and trade association, Jean-Claude Frankel, said on Thursday.
